playbook:
When a season begins, I check the stated sustainable share and take at or just under it unless I have a specific reason to deviate — keeping the stock high is what keeps future seasons profitable, and my final-season total was capped by early depletion.

In early seasons I do not over-harvest to "gain an edge." Grabbing a few extra fish early costs compounded regrowth across all remaining seasons and invites rivals to do the same; the small lead is never worth the shrinking pie.

When I see rivals consistently landing above the sustainable share, I raise my own catch slightly above my share to avoid subsidizing their greed — I don't get out-competed while alone preserving the commons.

I watch each season's landed figures, not just the stock. If everyone's share is near the sustainable number, I stay cooperative; if someone defects upward, I nudge up a point or two rather than matching their full defection, which would race the stock to zero.

In the final season, the stock no longer needs to regrow, so I push harder — taking above the sustainable share while still leaving margin in case rivals also ramp up, since a zeroed stock means nobody catches anything.

I never take so much that the stock could hit zero even if rivals overshoot; a collapse forfeits everything, which is strictly worse than a modest catch.

I keep a running idea of the terminal value: the last season's remaining stock divided among boats is roughly free fish, so I aim to arrive at the endgame with the stock healthy rather than grabbing early — the payoff of restraint shows up at the finish, not the start.

Playbook for catch (ref_commons):

- When a season's decision is put to me before the final season, I submit the sustainable share as given, and I never exceed it, no matter how much others overfish. Small defections by rivals (a few points above the share) don't destroy the stock; my defection adds nothing but risk.
- I don't try to punish or match overfishers. Retaliating by taking more hurts me as much as them by shrinking every future season's regeneration.
- I watch the stock trajectory, not just my rivals' catches. If the stock is declining season over season, I consider dropping slightly below the sustainable share only when the decline threatens collapse before the end — otherwise holding the share is enough.
- When the final season is put to me, I stop conserving and extract hard, since nothing left in the water scores. What didn't work last time: my final-season grab of 25 was too timid. With the stock at 85.7 and no future, I should have taken close to a full one-third of the stock (roughly 28–29), or even more once I account for likely rival restraint — the right amount is as much as is feasible without overshooting what remains, because fish left in the water at the end are worth zero.
- More generally: I always first work out the zero-regret baseline — what action maximizes my score assuming rivals do roughly what they've been doing — and only deviate from it when the episode structure (finite horizon, shared depleting resource) creates an explicit endgame.
- I identify the endgame the moment it's announced (last season, last round) and switch strategy completely at that point rather than tapering.
- I keep replies short and always end with the exact bracketed token required.

2.text:
- When the fishery opens and I have no information about the other boats, I submit exactly the sustainable share. It protects the stock, establishes me as cooperative, and costs little at a full stock.
- When the history shows all boats fishing sustainably, I keep fishing sustainably rather than being the first to defect — cooperation from everyone is worth more than a small grab.
- When one boat is overfishing and the stock shows it, I fish modestly above the sustainable share rather than either absorbing their defections passively or matching their escalation. A 10–15% overshoot closes the gap without visibly triggering a race.
- When I deviate above the sustainable share, I keep the overshoot small enough that it plausibly blends into the sustainable figures — others' reported catches show me nobody retaliated against my ~10–15% bumps, and I intend to preserve that cover.
- When the stock stays comfortably high with only a couple of seasons left, I loosen the restraint slightly again, because the remaining runway is the last value I can convert into catch.
- When the final season is put to me, I treat sustainability as worthless: remaining stock earns me nothing, so I submit the largest catch that cannot risk collapsing the stock to zero before my fish are counted. My final-season push was timid relative to the stock available — next time I take more of what's left, while still checking the regrowth arithmetic so I don't overshoot and get zero.
- When I calculate any season's catch, I first compute the total fishing pressure the recent history implies: if the other boats' current pace plus my planned catch would push the stock toward zero, I scale back regardless of my standing, because a collapsed fishery is a total loss.
- I do not chase rank by matching the largest other's catch; I chase total landed fish, and the record shows steady small edges plus a final-season surge beat that line.
